As founders compete to source the best and most cost effective talent for their startups, supporting remote workers becomes an increasingly attractive option.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eTo learn how to build an effective remote team we spoke to three founders who’ve mastered it: Joel Gascoigne of Buffer, Wade Foster of Zapier and Ben Halpern of Dev.to. It makes everyone feel more connected to the mission.\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch3\u003eAlign the team through performance metrics\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eAs Zapier’s remote team expanded, Wade realized he needed to do a lot more to keep the team on the same path focused on the customer needs. He spent 18 months developing a new OKR system to create alignment across all the different teams.\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch3\u003eExpect things to go wrong at first\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eAt Dev.to, Ben realized that perfecting remote working is a gradual thing, not something you get right at first. While some companies like Invision and Basecamp appear to have perfected the approach, many tech leaders remain dubious that it could work for their teams.</div><div>Competition for tech talent is fierce. As founders compete to source the best and most cost effective talent for their startups, supporting remote workers becomes an increasingly attractive option.</div><div>To learn how to build an effective remote team we spoke to three founders who’ve mastered it: Joel Gascoigne of Buffer, Wade Foster of Zapier and Ben Halpern of Dev.to. Subscribe to our weekly podcast <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/radio" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer">Product Hunt Radio</a> to hear the conversations in full. If you’re already a subscriber, please leave us a review on <a href="https://podcasts.apple.com/podcast/product-hunt-radio/id862714883" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer">Apple Podcasts</a>.</div><h3>Be transparent</h3><div>At Buffer, Joel’s approach is extreme transparency — he finds it fulfilling and liberating to be able to open up. He is direct and honest with his team and customers. It makes everyone feel more connected to the mission.</div><h3>Align the team through performance metrics</h3><div>As Zapier’s remote team expanded, Wade realized he needed to do a lot more to keep the team on the same path focused on the customer needs. He spent 18 months developing a new OKR system to create alignment across all the different teams.</div><h3>Expect things to go wrong at first</h3><div>At Dev.to, Ben realized that perfecting remote working is a gradual thing, not something you get right at first. For this reason it’s important to understand that things won’t be perfect at the start, but improve since you learn as you go.</div><h3>Let individuals optimize for their own productivity</h3><div>Ben reflected on how he used to love having the option to work from anywhere including coffeeshops but now prefers to have a home office with a desk his laptop stays on. Find what works for you and let others on your team do the same for themselves.</div><div><em>Subscribe to our weekly podcast </em><a href="https://www.producthunt.com/radio" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer"><em>Product Hunt Radio</em></a><em> to hear the conversations in full. https://www.producthunt.com/stories/4-ti.visible_text: 4 Tips to Help You Build an Effective Remote Team | Product Hunt Best Products Launches Launch archive Most-loved launches by the community Launch Guide Checklists and pro tips for launching News Newsletter The best of Product Hunt, every day Stories Tech news, interviews, and tips from makers Changelog New Product Hunt features and releases Forums Forums Ask questions, find support, and connect Kitty Points Leaderboard The highest scoring community members Streaks The most active community members Events Meet others online and in-person Advertise Subscribe Sign in Stories 4 Tips to Help You Build an Effective Remote Team We spoke to three founders who have mastered remote work. This is what they said. Abadesi September 12th, 2019 Remote work is a divisive topic in the tech world. While some companies like Invision and Basecamp appear to have perfected the approach, many tech leaders remain dubious that it could work for their teams. Competition for tech talent is fierce. As founders compete to source the best and most cost effective talent for their startups, supporting remote workers becomes an increasingly attractive option. To learn how to build an effective remote team we spoke to three founders who’ve mastered it: Joel Gascoigne of Buffer, Wade Foster of Zapier and Ben Halpern of Dev.to. Subscribe to our weekly podcast Product Hunt Radio to hear the conversations in full. If you’re already a subscriber, please leave us a review on Apple Podcasts . Be transparent At Buffer, Joel’s approach is extreme transparency — he finds it fulfilling and liberating to be able to open up. He is direct and honest with his team and customers. It makes everyone feel more connected to the mission. Align the team through performance metrics As Zapier’s remote team expanded, Wade realized he needed to do a lot more to keep the team on the same path focused on the customer needs. He spent 18 months developing a new OKR system to create alignment across all the different teams. Expect things to go wrong at first At Dev.to, Ben realized that perfecting remote working is a gradual thing, not something you get right at first. For this reason it’s important to understand that things won’t be perfect at the start, but improve since you learn as you go. Let individuals optimize for their own productivity Ben reflected on how he used to love having the option to work from anywhere including coffeeshops but now prefers to have a home office with a desk his laptop stays on. Find what works for you and let others on your team do the same for themselves. Subscribe to our weekly podcast Product Hunt Radio to hear the conversations in full. If you’re already a subscriber, please leave us a review on Apple Podcasts . Product Hunt engineering team has always been remote and it's surprisingly small for all the features and products we're shipping. One of our secret weapons is what we call \"collaborative single-player mode.\"\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eSingle-player mode is something I heard about for the first time from Andreas Klinger, the previous CTO of Product Hunt. He talks about it often. The core of the idea is simple: Everyone should be able to execute without depending on other people. Especially in a remote environment (when people work at different times), this is essential.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThe \"Collaborative\" prefix is my extension to \"Single Player\" to signify that we work as a team, not just as individuals.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThe following is copied and pasted from Product Hunt's engineering principles document and gives you a picture of how we execute on Collaborative Single Player Mode. 😎\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch2\u003eProcess\u003cbr\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eProcess is not about blindly following procedures. It is about:\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eMaking automatic decisions for trivial questions\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eEliminating blockers\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eMaking it obvious who owns which decision\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cem\u003eThe way we work is not set in stone. When you have ideas on how we can improve, share those with the team.\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://ph-files.imgix.net/1504c589-27f7-48f0-8706-ec79751f1f55.png?auto=format\u0026amp;auto=compress\u0026amp;codec=mozjpeg\u0026amp;cs=strip\" alt=\"\" /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eSingle-Player Mode\u003cbr\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eA developer should be able to execute a feature from start to finish — from the database to the backend, API, frontend, and CSS. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThe goal is never to get blocked.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf you are missing a design, mock the UI. Designers can fill this in later.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf you don't know how to do something technically, hack it or fake it.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf a product decision is missing, try to make this decision yourself. It's better to ask for forgiveness rather than permission\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch2\u003eEnablers for single-player mode\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eFor a sustainable work pace, and to produce a consistently high-quality product  in Single Player Mode, we have the following enablers:\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch3\u003eOwnership\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eYou own whatever you are working on. At Product Hunt, we treat people as capable, independent knowledge workers.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eIf you work on something, you drive decisions.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eTake a feature and find solutions\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ePull in people you need for feedback\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eSuggest solutions if you can\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3\u003eWhat should you work on?\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhenever you're unsure about what you should pick to work on, go for \"impact.\"\u003cbr\u003eWhat's can I work on right now that will have the greatest effect? Work on that.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003ch3\u003eSmall checkpoints\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eWe use trunk-driven development\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eA demo is worth a thousand words, and a working prototype is worth a hundred demos\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eGet feedback from the team early and often\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eTry to get the feature to production as quickly as possible\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eSplit feature into multiple smaller releasable features\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAlways start a feature with a feature flag and try to get something to production on day 1.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eeven if it's only feature flagged to you\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eusual feature flag timeline\u003c/li\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eweek 1 - developer and people interested in a feature\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eweek 2 - all admins\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eweek 3 - release or do beta with users\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003ch3\u003eCoding best practices\u003c/h3\u003eWe play in single-player, but collaboratively.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eFollow the coding rules\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAt least one fellow developer should see every code change\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWrite tests\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ePrefer explicit code\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWrite code as if you are going to remove it tomorrow\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf code style can't be enforced by linter, don't argue about it\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAutomate decisions\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eLook for places where reusable utilities or components can be extracted and used later\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWe do not optimize for speed or quality - we optimize our codebase for confidence\u003c/li\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eFor the next person to make changes\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eFor everyone to be able to reason about it\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eFor everyone to be informed enough to ask questions (leave your name next to notes)\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3\u003eThe scout rule\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eLeave the code cleaner than you found it.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eOr better said, pick up any trash lying on the floor.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e Clean up code as you go and develop more code. If you don't, you will find yourself in a mess shortly (much more likely than camping sites).\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eAny mistake left is now also your mistake\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAny \"wtf-moment\" you run into is a chance to avoid that for the next person (add notes, introduce best practices)\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf you can't take ownership, then we most likely have a more significant structural (process) problem at hand. Please address it to the team.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eDon't ask if you can refactor\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWe have an old application. Some of the rules and conditions of the system have changed, and the code doesn't always reflect that\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3\u003eData-driven decisions\u003cbr\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhen possible, always make sure you are backing your decisions with data.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eTry to validate if the feature is worth being developed\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eUse experiments to see if there is a demand for a feature\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAlways set up metrics for your features to make sure users use those as expected\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWhen I doubt do an A/B test\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eTry to understand the result from an A/B test and validate with follow up tests\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eOver the years, Product Hunt has changed a lot. There have been many products, processes, and team changes, but so far, these principles have stayed relatively stable.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eIf you have any questions or comments, Product Hunt engineering team has always been remote and it's surprisingly small for all the features and products we're shipping. One of our secret weapons is what we call \"collaborative single-player mode.\"\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eSingle-player mode is something I heard about for the first time from Andreas Klinger, the previous CTO of Product Hunt. He talks about it often. The core of the idea is simple: Everyone should be able to execute without depending on other people. Especially in a remote environment (when people work at different times), this is essential.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThe \"Collaborative\" prefix is my extension to \"Single Player\" to signify that we work as a team, not just as individuals.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThe following is copied and pasted from Product Hunt's engineering principles document and gives you a picture of how we execute on Collaborative Single Player Mode. 😎\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch2\u003eProcess\u003cbr\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eProcess is not about blindly following procedures. It is about:\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eMaking automatic decisions for trivial questions\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eEliminating blockers\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eMaking it obvious who owns which decision\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cem\u003eThe way we work is not set in stone. When you have ideas on how we can improve, share those with the team.\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://ph-files.imgix.net/1504c589-27f7-48f0-8706-ec79751f1f55.png?auto=format\u0026amp;auto=compress\u0026amp;codec=mozjpeg\u0026amp;cs=strip\" alt=\"\" /\u003e\u003cbr /\u003e\u003ch2\u003eSingle-Player Mode\u003cbr\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eA developer should be able to execute a feature from start to finish — from the database to the backend, API, frontend, and CSS. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThe goal is never to get blocked.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf you are missing a design, mock the UI. Designers can fill this in later.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf you don't know how to do something technically, hack it or fake it.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf a product decision is missing, try to make this decision yourself. It's better to ask for forgiveness rather than permission\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch2\u003eEnablers for single-player mode\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eFor a sustainable work pace, and to produce a consistently high-quality product  in Single Player Mode, we have the following enablers:\u003c/div\u003e\u003ch3\u003eOwnership\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eYou own whatever you are working on. At Product Hunt, we treat people as capable, independent knowledge workers.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eIf you work on something, you drive decisions.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eTake a feature and find solutions\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ePull in people you need for feedback\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eSuggest solutions if you can\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3\u003eWhat should you work on?\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhenever you're unsure about what you should pick to work on, go for \"impact.\"\u003cbr\u003eWhat's can I work on right now that will have the greatest effect? Work on that.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003ch3\u003eSmall checkpoints\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eWe use trunk-driven development\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eA demo is worth a thousand words, and a working prototype is worth a hundred demos\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eGet feedback from the team early and often\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eTry to get the feature to production as quickly as possible\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eSplit feature into multiple smaller releasable features\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAlways start a feature with a feature flag and try to get something to production on day 1.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eeven if it's only feature flagged to you\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eusual feature flag timeline\u003c/li\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eweek 1 - developer and people interested in a feature\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eweek 2 - all admins\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eweek 3 - release or do beta with users\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003ch3\u003eCoding best practices\u003c/h3\u003eWe play in single-player, but collaboratively.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eFollow the coding rules\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAt least one fellow developer should see every code change\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWrite tests\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ePrefer explicit code\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWrite code as if you are going to remove it tomorrow\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf code style can't be enforced by linter, don't argue about it\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAutomate decisions\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eLook for places where reusable utilities or components can be extracted and used later\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWe do not optimize for speed or quality - we optimize our codebase for confidence\u003c/li\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eFor the next person to make changes\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eFor everyone to be able to reason about it\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eFor everyone to be informed enough to ask questions (leave your name next to notes)\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3\u003eThe scout rule\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eLeave the code cleaner than you found it.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eOr better said, pick up any trash lying on the floor.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e Clean up code as you go and develop more code. If you don't, you will find yourself in a mess shortly (much more likely than camping sites).\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eAny mistake left is now also your mistake\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAny \"wtf-moment\" you run into is a chance to avoid that for the next person (add notes, introduce best practices)\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eIf you can't take ownership, then we most likely have a more significant structural (process) problem at hand. Please address it to the team.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eDon't ask if you can refactor\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWe have an old application. Some of the rules and conditions of the system have changed, and the code doesn't always reflect that\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3\u003eData-driven decisions\u003cbr\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhen possible, always make sure you are backing your decisions with data.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003eTry to validate if the feature is worth being developed\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eUse experiments to see if there is a demand for a feature\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAlways set up metrics for your features to make sure users use those as expected\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWhen I doubt do an A/B test\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eTry to understand the result from an A/B test and validate with follow up tests\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eOver the years, Product Hunt has changed a lot. There have been many products, processes, and team changes, but so far, these principles have stayed relatively stable.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eIf you have any questions or comments, sm:px-4"><div class="styles-module__HXdbxW__body" id="story-body"><div>The Product Hunt engineering team has always been remote and it's surprisingly small for all the features and products we're shipping. One of our secret weapons is what we call "collaborative single-player mode."</div><div>Single-player mode is something I heard about for the first time from Andreas Klinger, the previous CTO of Product Hunt. He talks about it often. The core of the idea is simple: Everyone should be able to execute without depending on other people. Especially in a remote environment (when people work at different times), this is essential.</div><div>The "Collaborative" prefix is my extension to "Single Player" to signify that we work as a team, not just as individuals.</div><div>The following is copied and pasted from Product Hunt's engineering principles document and gives you a picture of how we execute on Collaborative Single Player Mode. 😎</div><h2>Process<br></h2><div>Process is not about blindly following procedures. It is about:</div><ul><li>Making automatic decisions for trivial questions</li><li>Eliminating blockers</li><li>Making it obvious who owns which decision</li></ul><div><em>The way we work is not set in stone. When you have ideas on how we can improve, share those with the team.</em></div><img src="https://ph-files.imgix.net/1504c589-27f7-48f0-8706-ec79751f1f55.png?auto=format&auto=compress&codec=mozjpeg&cs=strip" alt="" /><br /><h2>Single-Player Mode<br></h2><div>A developer should be able to execute a feature from start to finish — from the database to the backend, API, frontend, and CSS. </div><div>The goal is never to get blocked.</div><ul><li>If you are missing a design, mock the UI. Designers can fill this in later.</li><li>If you don't know how to do something technically, hack it or fake it.</li><li>If a product decision is missing, try to make this decision yourself. It's better to ask for forgiveness rather than permission</li></ul><h2>Enablers for single-player mode</h2><div>For a sustainable work pace, and to produce a consistently high-quality product  in Single Player Mode, we have the following enablers:</div><h3>Ownership</h3><div>You own whatever you are working on. At Product Hunt, we treat people as capable, independent knowledge workers.</div><div>If you work on something, you drive decisions.</div><ul><li>Take a feature and find solutions</li><li>Pull in people you need for feedback</li><li>Suggest solutions if you can</li></ul><h3>What should you work on?</h3><div>Whenever you're unsure about what you should pick to work on, go for "impact."<br>What's can I work on right now that will have the greatest effect? Work on that.</div><div><h3>Small checkpoints</h3><ul><li>We use trunk-driven development</li><li>A demo is worth a thousand words, and a working prototype is worth a hundred demos</li><li>Get feedback from the team early and often</li><li>Try to get the feature to production as quickly as possible</li><li>Split feature into multiple smaller releasable features</li><li>Always start a feature with a feature flag and try to get something to production on day 1.</li><ul><li>even if it's only feature flagged to you</li><li>usual feature flag timeline</li><ul><li>week 1 - developer and people interested in a feature</li><li>week 2 - all admins</li><li>week 3 - release or do beta with users</li></ul></ul></ul></div><div><h3>Coding best practices</h3>We play in single-player, but collaboratively.</div><ul><li>Follow the coding rules</li><li>At least one fellow developer should see every code change</li><li>Write tests</li><li>Prefer explicit code</li><li>Write code as if you are going to remove it tomorrow</li><li>If code style can't be enforced by linter, don't argue about it</li><li>Automate decisions</li><li>Look for places where reusable utilities or components can be extracted and used later</li><li>We do not optimize for speed or quality - we optimize our codebase for confidence</li><ul><li>For the next person to make changes</li><li>For everyone to be able to reason about it</li><li>For everyone to be informed enough to ask questions (leave your name next to notes)</li></ul></ul><h3>The scout rule</h3><div>Leave the code cleaner than you found it.</div><div>Or better said, pick up any trash lying on the floor.<br><br> Clean up code as you go and develop more code. If you don't, you will find yourself in a mess shortly (much more likely than camping sites).</div><ul><li>Any mistake left is now also your mistake</li><li>Any "wtf-moment" you run into is a chance to avoid that for the next person (add notes, introduce best practices)</li><li>If you can't take ownership, then we most likely have a more significant structural (process) problem at hand. Please address it to the team.</li><li>Don't ask if you can refactor</li><li>We have an old application. Some of the rules and conditions of the system have changed, and the code doesn't always reflect that</li></ul><h3>Data-driven decisions<br></h3><div>When possible, always make sure you are backing your decisions with data.</div><ul><li>Try to validate if the feature is worth being developed</li><li>Use experiments to see if there is a demand for a feature</li><li>Always set up metrics for your features to make sure users use those as expected</li><li>When I doubt do an A/B test</li><li>Try to understand the result from an A/B test and validate with follow up tests</li></ul><div>Over the years, Product Hunt has changed a lot. There have been many products, processes, and team changes, but so far, these principles have stayed relatively stable.<br><br><br>If you have any questions or comments, you can ping me <a href="https://twitter.com/rstankov" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer">on Twitter</a>.</div></div></div></div><script https://www.producthunt.com/stories/how-.visible_text: How Product Hunt ships fast with a small, remote team | Product Hunt Best Products Launches Launch archive Most-loved launches by the community Launch Guide Checklists and pro tips for launching News Newsletter The best of Product Hunt, every day Stories Tech news, interviews, and tips from makers Changelog New Product Hunt features and releases Forums Forums Ask questions, find support, and connect Kitty Points Leaderboard The highest scoring community members Streaks The most active community members Events Meet others online and in-person Advertise Subscribe Sign in Stories How Product Hunt ships fast with a small, remote team Our secret weapon is what we call "collaborative single-player mode." Radoslav Stankov September 1st, 2021 The Product Hunt engineering team has always been remote and it's surprisingly small for all the features and products we're shipping. One of our secret weapons is what we call "collaborative single-player mode." Single-player mode is something I heard about for the first time from Andreas Klinger, the previous CTO of Product Hunt. He talks about it often. The core of the idea is simple: Everyone should be able to execute without depending on other people. Especially in a remote environment (when people work at different times), this is essential. The "Collaborative" prefix is my extension to "Single Player" to signify that we work as a team, not just as individuals. The following is copied and pasted from Product Hunt's engineering principles document and gives you a picture of how we execute on Collaborative Single Player Mode. 😎 Process Process is not about blindly following procedures. It is about: Making automatic decisions for trivial questions Eliminating blockers Making it obvious who owns which decision The way we work is not set in stone. When you have ideas on how we can improve, share those with the team. Single-Player Mode A developer should be able to execute a feature from start to finish — from the database to the backend, API, frontend, and CSS. The goal is never to get blocked. If you are missing a design, mock the UI. Designers can fill this in later. If you don't know how to do something technically, hack it or fake it. If a product decision is missing, try to make this decision yourself. It's better to ask for forgiveness rather than permission Enablers for single-player mode For a sustainable work pace, and to produce a consistently high-quality product in Single Player Mode, we have the following enablers: Ownership You own whatever you are working on. At Product Hunt, we treat people as capable, independent knowledge workers. If you work on something, you drive decisions. Take a feature and find solutions Pull in people you need for feedback Suggest solutions if you can What should you work on? Whenever you're unsure about what you should pick to work on, go for "impact." What's can I work on right now that will have the greatest effect? Work on that. Small checkpoints We use trunk-driven development A demo is worth a thousand words, and a working prototype is worth a hundred demos Get feedback from the team early and often Try to get the feature to production as quickly as possible Split feature into multiple smaller releasable features Always start a feature with a feature flag and try to get something to production on day 1. even if it's only feature flagged to you usual feature flag timeline week 1 - developer and people interested in a feature week 2 - all admins week 3 - release or do beta with users Coding best practices We play in single-player, but collaboratively. Follow the coding rules At least one fellow developer should see every code change Write tests Prefer explicit code Write code as if you are going to remove it tomorrow If code style can't be enforced by linter, don't argue about it Automate decisions Look for places where reusable utilities or components can be extracted and used later We do not optimize for speed or quality - we optimize our codebase for confidence For the next person to make changes For everyone to be able to reason about it For everyone to be informed enough to ask questions (leave your name next to notes) The scout rule Leave the code cleaner than you found it. Or better said, pick up any trash lying on the floor. Clean up code as you go and develop more code. If you don't, you will find yourself in a mess shortly (much more likely than camping sites). Any mistake left is now also your mistake Any "wtf-moment" you run into is a chance to avoid that for the next person (add notes, introduce best practices) If you can't take ownership, then we most likely have a more significant structural (process) problem at hand. Please address it to the team. Don't ask if you can refactor We have an old application. Some of the rules and conditions of the system have changed, and the code doesn't always reflect that Data-driven decisions When possible, always make sure you are backing your decisions with data. Try to validate if the feature is worth being developed Use experiments to see if there is a demand for a feature Always set up metrics for your features to make sure users use those as expected When I doubt do an A/B test Try to understand the result from an A/B test and validate with follow up tests Over the years, Product Hunt has changed a lot. There have been many products, processes, and team changes, but so far, these principles have stayed relatively stable. If you have any questions or comments, you can ping me on Twitter . a ton of job opportunities constantly being tweeted out there and as much as I tried to retweet them all, they still got lost in the feeds.” \u003c/em\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThis is the problem that led Makers Dann Petty and Chris Molitor to create a *different* type of job board — \u003ca href=\"https://www.producthunt.com/posts/epic-jobs\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003eEpic Jobs\u003c/a\u003e. 👀\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eHow it's unique: Epic Jobs sets itself apart from other job boards in that its listings feel human. Dann observed how personal tweets about open jobs garnered attention, and replicated that feeling on the platform. Job seekers can browse 90-140 second video clips called “Intros,” where they can learn about the opportunity directly from the hiring manager. The site also features “Office Tours,” which are fun videos that give you a virtual tour of a company's workspace. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eIt's worth noting that Epic didn't come to be overnight. In fact, Dann has been connecting people to jobs \u003ca href=\"https://twitter.com/KunalsLab/status/1121044273955246080\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003evia Twitter since 2010\u003c/a\u003e, and has been conducting experiments, polls and interviews about hiring along the way. It's a novel idea in a crowded — albeit difficult to crack — job hunting market. More from Dann and Chris themselves on launching the MVP, how to conduct research on social media and why they're excited about video. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat originally inspired you to start connecting folks to jobs via Twitter?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Twitter is great because it’s where a large part of our tech/creative community is. I’m a freelance designer and I relied heavily on Twitter to build, grow and maintain that community. You get a lot of job opportunities but can’t  take them all, so Twitter is a great place to share them with your friends and community. It’s all about connections and relationships. So that sharing mentality has been baked into my career since I started. Also, as the host of Epicurrence, an event for the tech industry, there was no better feeling than connecting people and hearing all the jobs that happened because of it. So I’ve been sharing jobs opportunities on Twitter and everywhere really for awhile now. I think a lot of us do.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat was the *aha* moment where you realized this needed to exist?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: I have this Tweet pinned to my Twitter that says:\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1089548230814248960\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eI tweeted that on a Sunday morning at 7:38 AM and it ended up getting over 1M impressions with 37K real engagements and hundreds and hundreds of jobs in it. I quickly realized how many people were sharing jobs via Twitter — it wasn’t just me. So, naturally, as a creator, I comped something up real quick only with the intention to make the tweets on that specific thread filterable and discoverable all on one page. That was it. It wasn’t until later I realized there could be something bigger.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat did your Twitter research look like? What were some key findings that influenced the product? \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: A lot of the research was looking to see how people were sharing their opportunities at their companies. Everyone had a link to the usual apply destinations or their career pages but there was nothing connecting all these Tweets together, and there wasn’t a great way to search for jobs on Twitter. After seeing how people were tweeting, we evaluated how we felt after going through all the job opportunities, and it felt best when we could see who was hiring. It felt best when we could actually see a person's photo, their name, how they tweet, etc. — it just made more sense. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhile you just get a logo and some text with most job boards, we wanted something more personal. You’re more likely to react to a person's face than a logo. Then it became obvious to us that we needed to take it a step further with video. We hadn't seen many video job descriptions out there, but we're trying to change that. We don’t know if it’ll work or not, but as a filmmaker, I’m obsessed with video right now.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eAlso, polls are absolutely incredible on Twitter. I’ve got such a responsive community on Twitter and I love how open they are to giving feedback quickly. I’ll ask random questions with a poll just to see what people think. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat was the hardest part of preparing to launch? What new skills did you have to learn?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: Having to stop the unending-process of polishing a product is definitely the hardest part of shipping. It's never 100% perfect or complete, but at some point you realize you're focusing on things people will likely never even notice. Being self-aware in this regard is always difficult. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhen planning the site architecture for epicjobs, we had to account for the fact that essentially all of the content was coming from either Twitter or YouTube. Utilizing those platform APIs and plugging it all into a seamless user experience was a unique challenge and something we’re continuing to explore as we grow the platform.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: To add to that, we had to keep remembering why we’re building this; it's literally just to get people jobs. It didn’t need to be fancy or perfect — it just needed to work.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHas your idea been validated? What's the response been like?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Oh, 100000 percent. We were not expecting this really. I mean you like to think your idea is great but actually hearing from others is just incredibly humbling.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121157506871377923\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121194990560927744\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121156298442018817\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121183286095536129\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat’s something you’ve unintentionally discovered while building Epic Jobs?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: The concept of “interviewing the interviewer” to learn about job opportunities seemed so simple and basic that I just assumed it was being done elsewhere. My initial thinking was the quality of these videos will stand out among the crowd. However, it didn’t take long for us to realize that this is not being done at all. It was very surprising (and a little confusing to be honest!). Why has this not been done yet?! \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat habits help you stay productive as a Maker? \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: COFFEE!!! Honestly though, managing your time and knowing when to turn off the screen is a big habit I’ve had to learn over the years. This helps keep interest fresh and prevents burnout.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Lots of breaks. Breaks help me focus. Whether just going outside or playing Fortnite — just taking a break from what you’re doing to let your mind rest and wonder is a great habit to get into.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eAlso Chris and I don’t get caught into email or Slack exchanges, we just text each other. Highly recommend. It’s a great habit to have with a friend you’re jamming on things with. You don’t always have to spin up a new Slack and things. Keep the friction low on communication because ultimately that’s what’s most important for your team.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat advice would you give Makers who want to conduct research on a social platform?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Just to do it. It’s free. Take advantage of the polls and don’t be afraid to ask your friends questions. There are a lot of tools out there for feedback but try to spend money when you don’t have to — utilize your networks first. Also make sure you thank people. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat's next for Epic Jobs?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: We’re going to continue providing job seekers insight into what employers are looking for through video intros, interviews and office tours. And we’re also excited to provide employers insight into job seekers as well. We’re in the planning stages now of expanding our services to include more information about our job seekers and their skills. Stay tuned! \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Yeah, we really want to become a great source to for connecting employees and job seekers in a more intimate, personal way. We want to be known as experts in job connections and in video. Whatever we need to do in order to accomplish that, that’s what’s next.\u003c/div\u003e","description":"Spoiler: the end result is more a ton of job opportunities constantly being tweeted out there and as much as I tried to retweet them all, they still got lost in the feeds.” \u003c/em\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eThis is the problem that led Makers Dann Petty and Chris Molitor to create a *different* type of job board — \u003ca href=\"https://www.producthunt.com/posts/epic-jobs\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003eEpic Jobs\u003c/a\u003e. 👀\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eHow it's unique: Epic Jobs sets itself apart from other job boards in that its listings feel human. Dann observed how personal tweets about open jobs garnered attention, and replicated that feeling on the platform. Job seekers can browse 90-140 second video clips called “Intros,” where they can learn about the opportunity directly from the hiring manager. The site also features “Office Tours,” which are fun videos that give you a virtual tour of a company's workspace. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eIt's worth noting that Epic didn't come to be overnight. In fact, Dann has been connecting people to jobs \u003ca href=\"https://twitter.com/KunalsLab/status/1121044273955246080\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow noopener noreferrer\"\u003evia Twitter since 2010\u003c/a\u003e, and has been conducting experiments, polls and interviews about hiring along the way. It's a novel idea in a crowded — albeit difficult to crack — job hunting market. More from Dann and Chris themselves on launching the MVP, how to conduct research on social media and why they're excited about video. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat originally inspired you to start connecting folks to jobs via Twitter?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Twitter is great because it’s where a large part of our tech/creative community is. I’m a freelance designer and I relied heavily on Twitter to build, grow and maintain that community. You get a lot of job opportunities but can’t  take them all, so Twitter is a great place to share them with your friends and community. It’s all about connections and relationships. So that sharing mentality has been baked into my career since I started. Also, as the host of Epicurrence, an event for the tech industry, there was no better feeling than connecting people and hearing all the jobs that happened because of it. So I’ve been sharing jobs opportunities on Twitter and everywhere really for awhile now. I think a lot of us do.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat was the *aha* moment where you realized this needed to exist?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: I have this Tweet pinned to my Twitter that says:\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1089548230814248960\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eI tweeted that on a Sunday morning at 7:38 AM and it ended up getting over 1M impressions with 37K real engagements and hundreds and hundreds of jobs in it. I quickly realized how many people were sharing jobs via Twitter — it wasn’t just me. So, naturally, as a creator, I comped something up real quick only with the intention to make the tweets on that specific thread filterable and discoverable all on one page. That was it. It wasn’t until later I realized there could be something bigger.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat did your Twitter research look like? What were some key findings that influenced the product? \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: A lot of the research was looking to see how people were sharing their opportunities at their companies. Everyone had a link to the usual apply destinations or their career pages but there was nothing connecting all these Tweets together, and there wasn’t a great way to search for jobs on Twitter. After seeing how people were tweeting, we evaluated how we felt after going through all the job opportunities, and it felt best when we could see who was hiring. It felt best when we could actually see a person's photo, their name, how they tweet, etc. — it just made more sense. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhile you just get a logo and some text with most job boards, we wanted something more personal. You’re more likely to react to a person's face than a logo. Then it became obvious to us that we needed to take it a step further with video. We hadn't seen many video job descriptions out there, but we're trying to change that. We don’t know if it’ll work or not, but as a filmmaker, I’m obsessed with video right now.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eAlso, polls are absolutely incredible on Twitter. I’ve got such a responsive community on Twitter and I love how open they are to giving feedback quickly. I’ll ask random questions with a poll just to see what people think. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat was the hardest part of preparing to launch? What new skills did you have to learn?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: Having to stop the unending-process of polishing a product is definitely the hardest part of shipping. It's never 100% perfect or complete, but at some point you realize you're focusing on things people will likely never even notice. Being self-aware in this regard is always difficult. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eWhen planning the site architecture for epicjobs, we had to account for the fact that essentially all of the content was coming from either Twitter or YouTube. Utilizing those platform APIs and plugging it all into a seamless user experience was a unique challenge and something we’re continuing to explore as we grow the platform.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: To add to that, we had to keep remembering why we’re building this; it's literally just to get people jobs. It didn’t need to be fancy or perfect — it just needed to work.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHas your idea been validated? What's the response been like?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Oh, 100000 percent. We were not expecting this really. I mean you like to think your idea is great but actually hearing from others is just incredibly humbling.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121157506871377923\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121194990560927744\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121156298442018817\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv data-tweet-id=\"1121183286095536129\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat’s something you’ve unintentionally discovered while building Epic Jobs?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: The concept of “interviewing the interviewer” to learn about job opportunities seemed so simple and basic that I just assumed it was being done elsewhere. My initial thinking was the quality of these videos will stand out among the crowd. However, it didn’t take long for us to realize that this is not being done at all. It was very surprising (and a little confusing to be honest!). Why has this not been done yet?! \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat habits help you stay productive as a Maker? \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: COFFEE!!! Honestly though, managing your time and knowing when to turn off the screen is a big habit I’ve had to learn over the years. This helps keep interest fresh and prevents burnout.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Lots of breaks. Breaks help me focus. Whether just going outside or playing Fortnite — just taking a break from what you’re doing to let your mind rest and wonder is a great habit to get into.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eAlso Chris and I don’t get caught into email or Slack exchanges, we just text each other. Highly recommend. It’s a great habit to have with a friend you’re jamming on things with. You don’t always have to spin up a new Slack and things. Keep the friction low on communication because ultimately that’s what’s most important for your team.\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat advice would you give Makers who want to conduct research on a social platform?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Just to do it. It’s free. Take advantage of the polls and don’t be afraid to ask your friends questions. There are a lot of tools out there for feedback but try to spend money when you don’t have to — utilize your networks first. Also make sure you thank people. \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat's next for Epic Jobs?\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eCM: We’re going to continue providing job seekers insight into what employers are looking for through video intros, interviews and office tours. And we’re also excited to provide employers insight into job seekers as well. We’re in the planning stages now of expanding our services to include more information about our job seekers and their skills. Stay tuned! \u003c/div\u003e\u003cdiv\u003eDP: Yeah, we really want to become a great source to for connecting employees and job seekers in a more intimate, personal way. We want to be known as experts in job connections and in video. Whatever we need to do in order to accomplish that, that’s what’s next.\u003c/div\u003e","description":"Spoiler: the end result is more class="my-8 flex flex-col gap-8 sm:px-4"><div class="styles-module__HXdbxW__body" id="story-body"><div><em>“There's a ton of job opportunities constantly being tweeted out there and as much as I tried to retweet them all, they still got lost in the feeds.” </em></div><div>This is the problem that led Makers Dann Petty and Chris Molitor to create a *different* type of job board — <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/posts/epic-jobs" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer">Epic Jobs</a>. 👀</div><div>How it's unique: Epic Jobs sets itself apart from other job boards in that its listings feel human. Dann observed how personal tweets about open jobs garnered attention, and replicated that feeling on the platform. Job seekers can browse 90-140 second video clips called “Intros,” where they can learn about the opportunity directly from the hiring manager. The site also features “Office Tours,” which are fun videos that give you a virtual tour of a company's workspace. </div><div>It's worth noting that Epic didn't come to be overnight. In fact, Dann has been connecting people to jobs <a href="https://twitter.com/KunalsLab/status/1121044273955246080" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener noreferrer">via Twitter since 2010</a>, and has been conducting experiments, polls and interviews about hiring along the way. It's a novel idea in a crowded — albeit difficult to crack — job hunting market. More from Dann and Chris themselves on launching the MVP, how to conduct research on social media and why they're excited about video. </div><div><strong>What originally inspired you to start connecting folks to jobs via Twitter?</strong></div><div>DP: Twitter is great because it’s where a large part of our tech/creative community is. I’m a freelance designer and I relied heavily on Twitter to build, grow and maintain that community. You get a lot of job opportunities but can’t  take them all, so Twitter is a great place to share them with your friends and community. It’s all about connections and relationships. So that sharing mentality has been baked into my career since I started. Also, as the host of Epicurrence, an event for the tech industry, there was no better feeling than connecting people and hearing all the jobs that happened because of it. So I’ve been sharing jobs opportunities on Twitter and everywhere really for awhile now. I think a lot of us do.</div><div><strong>What was the *aha* moment where you realized this needed to exist?</strong></div><div>DP: I have this Tweet pinned to my Twitter that says:</div><div data-tweet-id="1089548230814248960"></div><div>I tweeted that on a Sunday morning at 7:38 AM and it ended up getting over 1M impressions with 37K real engagements and hundreds and hundreds of jobs in it. I quickly realized how many people were sharing jobs via Twitter — it wasn’t just me. So, naturally, as a creator, I comped something up real quick only with the intention to make the tweets on that specific thread filterable and discoverable all on one page. That was it. It wasn’t until later I realized there could be something bigger.</div><div><strong>What did your Twitter research look like? What were some key findings that influenced the product? </strong></div><div>DP: A lot of the research was looking to see how people were sharing their opportunities at their companies. Everyone had a link to the usual apply destinations or their career pages but there was nothing connecting all these Tweets together, and there wasn’t a great way to search for jobs on Twitter. After seeing how people were tweeting, we evaluated how we felt after going through all the job opportunities, and it felt best when we could see who was hiring. It felt best when we could actually see a person's photo, their name, how they tweet, etc. — it just made more sense. </div><div>While you just get a logo and some text with most job boards, we wanted something more personal. You’re more likely to react to a person's face than a logo. Then it became obvious to us that we needed to take it a step further with video. We hadn't seen many video job descriptions out there, but we're trying to change that. We don’t know if it’ll work or not, but as a filmmaker, I’m obsessed with video right now.</div><div>Also, polls are absolutely incredible on Twitter. I’ve got such a responsive community on Twitter and I love how open they are to giving feedback quickly. I’ll ask random questions with a poll just to see what people think. </div><div><strong>What was the hardest part of preparing to launch? What new skills did you have to learn?</strong></div><div>CM: Having to stop the unending-process of polishing a product is definitely the hardest part of shipping. It's never 100% perfect or complete, but at some point you realize you're focusing on things people will likely never even notice. Being self-aware in this regard is always difficult. </div><div>When planning the site architecture for epicjobs, we had to account for the fact that essentially all of the content was coming from either Twitter or YouTube. Utilizing those platform APIs and plugging it all into a seamless user experience was a unique challenge and something we’re continuing to explore as we grow the platform.</div><div>DP: To add to that, we had to keep remembering why we’re building this; it's literally just to get people jobs. It didn’t need to be fancy or perfect — it just needed to work.</div><div><strong>Has your idea been validated? What's the response been like?</strong></div><div>DP: Oh, 100000 percent. We were not expecting this really. I mean you like to think your idea is great but actually hearing from others is just incredibly humbling.</div><div data-tweet-id="1121157506871377923"></div><div data-tweet-id="1121194990560927744"></div><div data-tweet-id="1121156298442018817"></div><div data-tweet-id="1121183286095536129"></div><div><strong>What’s something you’ve unintentionally discovered while building Epic Jobs?</strong></div><div>CM: The concept of “interviewing the interviewer” to learn about job opportunities seemed so simple and basic that I just assumed it was being done elsewhere. My initial thinking was the quality of these videos will stand out among the crowd. However, it didn’t take long for us to realize that this is not being done at all. It was very surprising (and a little confusing to be honest!). Why has this not been done yet?! </div><div><strong>What habits help you stay productive as a Maker? </strong></div><div>CM: COFFEE!!! Honestly though, managing your time and knowing when to turn off the screen is a big habit I’ve had to learn over the years. This helps keep interest fresh and prevents burnout.</div><div>DP: Lots of breaks. Breaks help me focus. Whether just going outside or playing Fortnite — just taking a break from what you’re doing to let your mind rest and wonder is a great habit to get into.</div><div>Also Chris and I don’t get caught into email or Slack exchanges, we just text each other. Highly recommend. It’s a great habit to have with a friend you’re jamming on things with. You don’t always have to spin up a new Slack and things. Keep the friction low on communication because ultimately that’s what’s most important for your team.</div><div><strong>What advice would you give Makers who want to conduct research on a social platform?</strong></div><div>DP: Just to do it. It’s free. Take advantage of the polls and don’t be afraid to ask your friends questions. There are a lot of tools out there for feedback but try to spend money when you don’t have to — utilize your networks first. Also make sure you thank people. </div><div><strong>What's next for Epic Jobs?</strong></div><div>CM: We’re going to continue providing job seekers insight into what employers are looking for through video intros, interviews and office tours. And we’re also excited to provide employers insight into job seekers as well. We’re in the planning stages now of expanding our services to include more information about our job seekers and their skills. Stay tuned! </div><div>DP: Yeah, we really want to become a great source to for connecting employees and job seekers in a more intimate, personal way. We want to be known as experts in job connections and in video. Whatever we need to do in order to accomplish that, that’s what’s next.</div></div></div></div><script
